summary: Shoppers first choose between a magnetic (Hall effect or TMR) board for competitive games and a mechanical board for typing, then cut by budget ($50, $100, $150 and $200 are the tiers they search), by number pad or compact layout, and by low profile, wireless and noise. Since late September the Wooting 80HE+ started shipping, Keychron listed an Ultra 8K line that claims 8,000 Hz over 2.4 GHz, and Black Friday prices put the Keychron K3 HE ($95.99) and Epomaker HE65 V2 TMR ($59.99) under lines our pages hold. Our cheapest pick, the Gamakay NS68, shows out of stock on all eight variants today (2026-11-27), which empties our two under-$50 pages.

axes.label: Magnetic (Hall effect or TMR) switches or ordinary mechanical ones
axes.why: The first question ChatGPT asked (4 of 6 chats, per the brief) is use: it sends competitive gaming to magnetic boards and typing to mechanical ones. HLPlanet's guide (dated 2026-10-26) treats adjustable actuation, rapid trigger, Snap Tap and hot-swap as the base feature set of every magnetic board it lists. Search suggestions carry separate 'hall effect', 'tmr' and 'rapid trigger' families.

breakpoints.why: Magnetic sensing is what makes per-key adjustable actuation and rapid trigger possible; Wooting states 0.1 to 4.0 mm per key on the 80HE.

A different sensor type that shoppers search by name (suggestions: 'best tmr keyboard wireless', 'budget', 'under 100'); Epomaker claims lower latency and lower power draw than Hall sensors (maker claim).

A rule: Engadget (2024-08-20) reports Valve kicks players from official Counter-Strike 2 matches when SOCD features such as Razer Snap Tap or Wooting Snappy Tappy are detected, so it is not a selling point for CS2.

axes.label: Silent switches for a shared room
axes.why: ChatGPT asked about a shared office in 2 of 6 chats and told shoppers to pick explicitly silent switches (brief). HLPlanet has a 'silent' category. Our silent Hall effect page is the cluster's most visited (14 visits, 1 sale).

axes.label: Measured input delay
axes.why: HLPlanet ranks a 'best latency' group on its own OSLTT readings, which is the only like-for-like figure across brands; maker figures are report intervals.

breakpoints.why: Every board HLPlanet puts a number on sits below 1 ms by cable: ATK RS6 0.16, MCHOSE Ace 68 0.3, Luminkey Magger 68 0.35, Wooting 80HE 0.42, Womier SK75 TMR 0.5, MelGeek Centauri 80 0.53.

axes.label: Polling rate
axes.why: ChatGPT named 1,000 Hz as the K2 HE's main compromise against the 8,000 Hz Wooting (brief); makers put 8K in product titles.

breakpoints.why: USB low and full speed divide bus time into 1 ms frames.
USB high speed adds 125 µs microframes, eight per 1 ms frame; '0.125 ms latency' on listings is this interval, not a measurement.
MCHOSE now sells boards rated 'up to 16K', so 8K is no longer the highest printed figure.

axes.label: Shortest actuation and rapid trigger step
axes.why: Makers headline it (0.01, 0.005, 0.001 mm); Wooting and Keychron publish plainer ranges, so a comparison has to say whose statement each is.

breakpoints.why: Wooting's stated floor and step (0.1 to 4.0 mm in 0.1 mm steps); Keychron's Gateron-switch boards start at 0.2 mm.
Budget makers print adjustment precision, not a tested minimum: MCHOSE Ace 68 'up to 0.001 mm RT accuracy', Epomaker HE68 Lite 'per 0.01mm'.

axes.label: Which replacement switches fit
axes.why: ChatGPT asked whether the configuration is hot-swappable (brief). Magnetic sockets are not interchangeable across brands.

breakpoints.why: Keychron says its HE boards take only Gateron Double-Rail (or Keychron Lime) switches, not Gateron Jade or KS-20; Gamakay says its V1 magnetic switches work only in the TK75HE V1.
Epomaker's TMR boards accept both kinds in the same socket.

axes.label: Aluminum or plastic case
axes.why: ChatGPT offered 'typing feel and an aluminum case' against versatility in 2 of 6 chats (brief); Lofree prices on it (Flow 2 aluminum $139 to $169, Flow Lite 2 plastic $109 to $119).

breakpoints.why: Lofree's Flow 2 is milled from a single block of aluminum and costs $50 more than the plastic Flow Lite 2 at the same size.

axes.label: Knob or screen
axes.why: Google completes 'hall effect keyboard with' first with screen, knob and volume knob.

breakpoints.why: Rare on magnetic boards and expensive: Turtle Beach KB7 $200 (4.3-inch touch display), MelGeek Centauri 80 $399 (1.78-inch OLED).
Available from $63.99 (Gamakay NS75), so it splits otherwise similar 75% boards.

rules: Hall effect and TMR are both magnetic sensing; 'mechanical' on a listing title does not exclude either, and Gamakay's Freewolf boards are 'mechanical feeling' membrane keyboards. A maker's '0.125 ms latency' is the 8,000 Hz report interval, and '0.01', '0.005' or '0.001 mm' is adjustment precision; neither is a measurement. The only like-for-like latency figures read for this map are HLPlanet's OSLTT readings, quoted by name. '8K' has to be stated per connection: Yunzii prints 8K on 2.4 GHz with 1 ms latency, Keychron's HE boards are 1,000 Hz on every connection, and Bluetooth is slower again. Wooting states a 0.1 mm floor and Keychron 0.2 mm, so maker ranges are not comparable with precision claims. Magnetic switch sockets are brand-specific (Keychron: Gateron Double-Rail only; Gamakay V1 switches fit only the TK75HE V1). Low-profile magnetic boards have shorter travel (0.2 to 2.9 mm on the K3 HE). Battery hours assume the backlight is off. Snap Tap is not an advantage in Counter-Strike 2, where Valve kicks for it. Prices move weekly; every price needs its read date, and Lofree's checkout discount has to be re-checked per product.
